title: Contact
summary: Build voluntary eye contact, check-ins, and handler connection without nagging.

subcategories.title: Contact 1,2,3
subcategories.goal: Contact 1, 2, 3 is a simple positive reinforcement exercise that teaches your dog to regularly check in with you and pay attention during walks and training. The goal is not to force eye contact. Instead, we create a habit where your dog learns that looking at you is valuable.
subcategories.steps:
Contact 1 – Building the Behaviour
Goal

Teach your dog that looking at you earns a reward.

Method
Start in a quiet environment.
Wait silently.
The moment your dog looks at your face:
Mark ("Yes!")
Reward

Repeat many times.

Your dog begins to learn:

"Looking at my human makes good things happen."

Success Criteria

Your dog is voluntarily offering eye contact several times within a minute.

Contact 2 – Adding Duration
Goal

Teach your dog to maintain attention for slightly longer.

Method

Instead of rewarding immediately:

Dog looks at you
Count:
One second
Mark
Reward

Gradually increase to:

Two seconds
Three seconds
Five seconds

Build slowly.

Success Criteria

Your dog can comfortably maintain eye contact for several seconds without frustration.

Contact 3 – Adding Distractions
Goal

Teach your dog to choose you even when interesting things are happening.

Method

Practice in increasingly challenging environments:

Garden
Quiet street
Park
Around people
Around dogs

Start far away from distractions.

When your dog notices something and then looks back at you:

Mark
Reward generously

The dog learns:

"Checking in with my human is always worth it."

Success Criteria

Your dog voluntarily offers attention despite environmental distractions.

Real-Life Application

Use Contact 1, 2, 3 throughout everyday life:

Before crossing roads
Before greeting people
Before greeting dogs
During loose leash walking
Before releasing to sniff
Before opening doors

This creates a dog that naturally checks in rather than needing constant commands.

Common Mistakes

❌ Repeating the dog's name constantly

❌ Demanding eye contact for too long

❌ Practicing near distractions too early

❌ Only rewarding with food and never using real-life rewards

❌ Progressing faster than the dog is ready for

Simple Progression

Contact 1
→ Dog looks at you

Contact 2
→ Dog maintains attention

Contact 3
→ Dog chooses you around distractions

The beauty of Contact 1, 2, 3 is that it develops engagement voluntarily. Instead of repeatedly asking for attention, your dog learns that paying attention to you is one of the most rewarding things they can do.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Reward voluntary, relaxed check-ins. A glance towards you is enough; never insist on prolonged eye contact or physically position the head. Reduce distractions if the dog struggles and let them look away freely.

subcategories.title: Watch Me on Cue — Battersea
subcategories.goal: Teach a gentle cue for a brief, comfortable look towards the handler.
subcategories.steps: Begin indoors with small treats. Hold a treat to the side and mark the moment the dog looks back towards your face, then reward. Once the response is predictable, say Watch me before presenting the hand. Gradually add a brief pause before rewarding.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Keep the first looks very short and release the dog between repetitions. Nervous dogs may find direct eye contact uncomfortable; accept orientation towards you and avoid staring at them.

subcategories.title: Eye Contact and Reward Timing — Training Positive
subcategories.goal: Improve voluntary attention and clear marker-and-reward timing.
subcategories.steps: Choose a quiet setting and prepare small food rewards. Mark a brief voluntary look towards you, then deliver the reward. Reset between repetitions so the dog can choose to reorient. Repeat easy successes before adding a little duration or changing your hand position.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Every marker should be followed by a reward. Avoid holding food out of reach for prolonged periods or waiting through frustration. Make the task easier if the dog disengages.

subcategories.title: Responding to a Name or Attention Sound — Kikopup
subcategories.goal: Build a positive response when the handler asks for attention.
subcategories.steps: Choose one friendly attention sound or the dog’s name. In a quiet room, pair it with a reward. When the dog begins turning towards you, mark the turn and reward. Practise from different positions before introducing mild distractions at a comfortable distance.
subcategories.coachingNotes: Use the cue once and allow time to respond. Avoid using the name to scold or repeating it continuously. Orientation is useful contact; prolonged staring is unnecessary.

subcategories.title: Keeping Contact Around Mild Distractions — Training Positive
subcategories.goal: Help familiar attention skills transfer to gradually more interesting settings.
subcategories.steps: Start where the dog can easily offer a check-in. Add a small, predictable distraction at a generous distance and reward reconnection with you. Change only one difficulty at a time, such as distance or movement. Keep sessions brief and allow breaks for safe exploration.
subcategories.coachingNotes: If attention becomes difficult, increase distance or reduce the distraction. Do not use lead corrections or demand eye contact when the dog is frightened. This is attention practice; use the Reactivity Training lessons for emotional responses to triggers.
